Moor HouseSchool & College
A specialist school & collegefor children & young people with language disorders.
Moor House School
Moor House School is a charity and non-maintained speech and language specialist school for day and residential students aged 7-19, with placements funded by Local Education Authorities nationwide. We deliver a mainstream curriculum adapted for language needs, with speech and language therapy fully integrated throughout your child’s education. This approach helps students reach their learning potential, build confident communication skills, and grow into happy, independent members of society. Moor House is consistently rated Outstanding by Ofsted.
Moor House College
Moor House College is the co-educational sixth form provision of Moor House School, offering both day and weekly residential placements. Students continue to receive individualised Speech and Language Therapy intervention delivered in 1:1 sessions, small groups and direct classroom support. Occupational Therapy, Physiotherapy, Psychotherapy and Specialist Literacy interventions also continue and are embedded across the curriculum.
Moor House Residential
Moor House Residential offers both day and weekly residential placements for students in year 6 upwards. Our residential provision offers a warm, friendly and inclusive environment where pastoral care and student wellbeing are central to daily life. We aim to create a supportive community in which young people feel safe, valued and able to grow with confidence.
Moor House Research & Training Institute
Moor House Research & Training Institute is a globally recognised centre advancing research, training and resources in speech, language and communication needs, particularly Developmental Language Disorder (DLD). Part of Moor House School & College, it drives evidence-led practice that informs high-quality interventions used in education and clinical settings, led by specialist researchers and clinicians.
Our Story & History
Before it became a school, the original Moor House was owned by the Clutton-Brocks family. During World War 2 it was home to Canadian Air Force Pilots and, later, Italian prisoners of war who worked on local farms.
Dr Cecil Charles Worster-Drought was a neurologist of world renown and Medical Director at the West End Hospital for Nervous Diseases in London. Speech Therapist Mrs Silvia Hudson-Smith was a founder and the first Principal of Moor House until her retirement in 1966.
Moor House opened to students on 21st April 1947 with 21 students aged 5-11 attending by the end of that month. The school was later officially opened by the Right Hon, George Tomlinson, Minister for Education, on 28th June 1947.
An extension comprising classrooms, offices and storage space was added to Moor House in 1951, enabling the number of pupils to rise to 50, also extending the upper age limit to 16.
Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother visited Moor House on 26th November 1953. Her visit was a great success and later, in 1957, she agreed to become the schools Patron. As a consequence, Her Majesty would send a large box of chocolates as a gift to the children each Christmas.
Major building projects
Further extensions including an assembly hall and common rooms, followed by a speech therapy clinic and house for the Principal were completed in 1959 and 1961 respectively, allowing the number of students to rise again to 61.
Swimming pool and fete takings
An outdoor swimming pool was added in 1969 and completed in time for the school fete that year, which raised 782 pounds, 9 shillings and 6 pence.
Main building replaces original Moor House
By 1972, work had also begun on the main quadrangle building we know today. It was a complex, phased build, with three sides complete by 1973 before the old House was demolished and the fourth side added later. The building was officially opened by former Minister of Education Lord Boyle of Handsworth on 24th June 1975.
Parade to celebrate Queen Mother’s 90th birthday
In 1990, Moor House students took part in a parade as part of celebrations for the 90th birthday of our Patron, Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother.
Jubilee celebrations
A Jubilee Fete was held in 1997 to mark the school’s fiftieth anniversary attended my many former pupils, including some of the very first students from 1947. Current and former Principals Mr Flaherty, Mr Lea and Mr Robertson cut the cake!
‘The Countess makes their day’
HRH The Countess of Wessex GCVO succeeded Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother as our Patron and visited the school in successive years in 2003 and 2004 to open a new assessment centre and the new sports and drama centre respectively. In 2011 the School welcomed day students for the first time in its history. Initially, 7 new day students joined 73 boarders. Moor House College opened in 2012, providing sixth form education for the first time alongside a number of partner colleges.
The opening of a college required more residential space, so John Lea House, a residential building for post-16 students named after our former school Principal, was completed in 2012 and officially opened by our Patron The Countess of Wessex.
Our residential campus for junior students, known as ‘The Village’ was completed in May 2016, providing 40 student bedrooms, 3 communal kitchens and dining areas, a Medical & Care Centre and a multi-purpose Student Centre.
Specialist Teaching and Therapy Hub
As we celebrate 75 years Moor House continues to look to the future with the completion of a new, two storey Specialist Therapy Hub.

pageCache.text:
A Winning Moment of Kindness
Other News
We are delighted to share some heart‑warming news from our local community.
Mrs. Wendy Hamm, a supporter of our school, recently won £250 in the Tandridge Together Lottery, and immediately chose to donate the entire amount back to us.
Her generous contribution has been kindly directed to support our College residential provision, helping us enrich the experiences of our older students.
On behalf of everyone at Moor House School & College, thank you, Wendy.
About the Tandridge Together Lottery
For those unfamiliar with the initiative, the Tandridge Together Lottery is a weekly community fundraising lottery open to local residents. A remarkable 60% of every ticket sold goes directly toward good causes in the Tandridge district, with players able to nominate a charity, such as Moor House, to receive 50p of every £1 they spend.
Tickets cost just £1 per week, and each has a 1 in 50 chance of winning a prize. Every Saturday night, a six‑digit combination is drawn, with awards ranging from free extra tickets to £25,000 for matching all six numbers.
Compared to national draws, the odds of winning are significantly improved, making it a fun and rewarding way to support the community.
If you’d like to learn more about the Tandridge Together Lottery or choose Moor House as your supported cause, you can find details on the lottery website.
2 matches: 3 extra tickets

pageCache.pageTitle: Moor House Student Champions DLD Awareness in Parliament  - Moor House School & College
pageCache.text:
Moor House Student Champions DLD Awareness in Parliament
Other News
Young people demonstrated the power of advocacy at a Young People’s Committee for Speech, Language and Communication, held at Parliament on Tuesday 23 June 2026.
The event, organised by the Speech, Language and Communication Alliance, offered a unique platform for young people to share their experiences and ask questions with MPs including Jen Craft, Helen Hayes, Jess Phillips and Saqib Bhatti.
Among them was Maxwell Letts, a student at Moor House School & College, who spoke honestly and passionately about his lived experience of Developmental Language Disorder (DLD), and his wish for greater awareness, asking MP’s ‘how are you going to raise the profile of DLD and spread awareness so more people know about it?’
Following the event, Maxwell also took the initiative to write to the MPs he met, reinforcing his message and highlighted a key issue that currently 80% of teacher are not aware of DLD.
Maxwell also encouraged the MPs to fulfil their commitment to raise awareness and asked for further engagement on how DLD can be better understood and supported nationwide.
Moor House School & College is incredibly proud of Maxwell and all the young people who contributed to this important event. Their willingness to speak out, share their experiences, and advocate for change is truly inspiring. His actions are helping to raise awareness, challenge misconceptions, and push for better support in education and beyond.
For more information on DLD visit our dedicated page on the Moor House Research & Training Institute website WHAT IS DLD? – Moor House Research & Training Institute
You can also hear from Maxwell, who was a recent guest (episode 5) on the DLD DownLoaD Podcast DLD PODCAST – Moor House Research & Training Institute

pageCache.pageTitle: Fete Brings Moor House Community Together - Moor House School & College
pageCache.text:
Fete Brings Moor House Community Together
Other News
This year’s Moor House Summer Fete was a tremendous success, bringing together students, families and staff for a wonderful afternoon of fun, fundraising and community spirit.
In a change from previous years, the fete was held on a school day. The decision was made to ensure that all current students could take part, including those who travel significant distances to attend Moor House and who might otherwise never have had the opportunity to experience the annual fete. As a result, many students were able to enjoy the event for the very first time alongside their classmates.
We were fortunate to enjoy fantastic weather throughout the afternoon, creating the perfect setting for families and students to come together and enjoy the wide range of activities on offer. The school grounds were filled with laughter, conversation and a real sense of community as visitors explored the stalls, enjoyed the barbecue and tried their luck in the raffle.
A particular highlight was the enthusiasm and creativity shown by our students. Class teams took ownership of planning, preparing and running many of the stalls, developing valuable skills in teamwork, organisation, communication and problem-solving. Students worked hard behind the scenes in the weeks leading up to the event and took great pride in seeing their ideas come to life on the day.
We were delighted to welcome so many families to the fete and are extremely grateful for the support shown by everyone who attended, volunteered, donated prizes or contributed in any way.
The event also proved to be a fantastic fundraising success, generating an impressive £4,651.47 before expenses.
Events like the Summer Fete remind us of the strength of the Moor House community and the positive impact that can be achieved when students, families, staff and supporters come together. Thank you to everyone who helped make the day such a memorable occasion. We are already looking forward to next year’s celebration.

Friends of Moor House
Friends of Moor House
Friends of Moor House is a welcoming voluntary association for anyone with an interest in Moor House School & College. There are no membership fees and no obligations. It is simply an opportunity to stay connected, support our students, and be part of our community.
We are particularly delighted to welcome:
You don’t need a previous connection with Moor House to join, just an interest in seeing our young people thrive.
Former students and their families
Current and former staff
Local residents
What we do
Friends of Moor House supports the School & College in practical, positive ways that enrich student life and strengthen community links. Our members have:
In our foundation year (2018-19) we introduced two annual awards, one each for the school and college, recognising students who have shown outstanding commitment to the wider community.
Members receive a termly newsletter with updates from across the School & College and are occasionally invited to open mornings and tours to see our work first-hand.

Curriculum
Students study a broad, balanced and differentiated curriculum, incorporating the requirements of their chosen vocational courses as well as Maths, English and PSHCE qualifications. These are highly modified in language content and presentation, to ensure our students significant language needs are met. Students have the opportunity to undertake work experience placements and follow a study skills programme as part of the curriculum. At Moor House College the specialised approaches required to develop language are integrated throughout the whole teaching day supported with a range of specialist visual systems and strategies (for example SHAPE CODING ™, Cued Articulation, and signing with grammatical markers), which are implemented across the college day. All our students have an individualised therapeutic programme of life and social skills as well as independence training (using the WHEEL OF INDEPENDENCE™ and the Travel Training system) which operates across the week and into the evenings working towards becoming independent adults.
Post‑16: Preparing for Adult Life
Our Post‑16 provision is designed to help students transition confidently into adulthood.
Individual study programmes may include:
Every learner is supported to identify aspirations and work towards a fulfilling future.
Academic or vocational qualifications
Work‑related learning and real‑world experiences
Independent living and community skills
Ongoing development of communication, self‑advocacy and resilience

Curriculum
An Individualised Curriculum That Unlocks Potential
At Moor House School & College, our curriculum is designed to do more than deliver learning—it transforms futures.
Specialising in supporting children and young people with speech, language and communication needs (DLD) we offer a personalised, therapeutic and ambitious curriculum from Key stage 2 through to Post‑16. Every pupil follows an individualised pathway that builds confidence, communication, independence and achievement.
Our curriculum evolves as pupils grow, ensuring they are supported, challenged and inspired at every stage.
Our curriculum focuses on:
Small steps are celebrated, confidence grows, and pupils begin to see themselves as successful learners.
Key Stage 2 (Years 3–6): Building Skills and Growing Independence
As pupils move through Key Stage 2, they deepen their skills and broaden their experiences.
Pupils are encouraged to take increasing ownership of their learning while receiving the support they need to succeed.

pageCache.pageTitle: Speech and Language Therapy - Moor House School & College
pageCache.text:
Speech and Language Therapy
Speech and Language Therapy On-Site
Moor House has an extensive and highly specialist team of onsite Speech and Language Therapists (SLTs). Each therapist works with a small caseload of up to 12 students throughout the academic year, allowing for consistent, personalised support. SLTs provide intensive intervention through individual sessions and small‑group work, carefully targeting each student’s specific language and communication needs.
Our school based SLTs work directly within the classroom environment. Lessons, including subjects such as English and Science, are jointly planned and delivered alongside specialist teachers who have extensive experience supporting students with language impairment. At college level, our SLTs collaborate closely with partner colleges, offering off‑site training, support and specialist advice within further education settings.
Speech and Language Frameworks Embedded in Curriculum
All intervention is continuously evaluated to ensure effectiveness, and our SLT team shares its findings nationally. We deliver intensive, evidence-based intervention using highly specialist speech and language frameworks embedded throughout the curriculum, including SHAPE CODING™, Sign‑Supported English with grammatical markers, and Cued Articulation. Alongside their expertise in language development and intervention, our therapists also specialise in speech sound disorders, which often co‑occur with language difficulties.
Dedicated Therapeutic Centre
Moor House is home to a dedicated therapeutic centre for students with severe speech sound disorders. This centre is equipped with advanced specialist technology, including Electropalatography (EPG) and ultrasound biofeedback. Our SLT team also uses highly specialised therapeutic approaches such as Dynamic Temporal and Tactile Cueing (DTTC) and Prompts for Restructuring Oral Muscular Phonetic Targets (PROMPT).
Students at Moor House make outstanding progress on standardised speech and language assessments throughout their time with us, significantly narrowing the gap between themselves and their typically developing peers.
Partnerships
We maintain strong partnerships with universities, supporting trainee therapists and collaborating on joint research projects to ensure our students benefit from the most effective and up-to-date practice.
International Recognition
Our therapeutic approaches are recognised internationally, and we are frequently invited to share our expertise. Through our Research Institute, we ensure that our speech and language therapy methodology for children with language disorders remains at the forefront of national and international practice.

Moor House Residential
Our residential provision offers a warm, friendly and inclusive environment where pastoral care and student wellbeing are central to daily life. We aim to create a supportive community in which young people feel safe, valued and able to grow with confidence.
Each residential house provides modern, comfortable single bedrooms alongside shared living spaces that encourages social interaction and the development of life skills. This structure enables students to thrive both academically and socially, supported by a dedicated team of residential staff and surrounded by peers who understand and share their experiences.
Most students board from Monday to Friday, though we can also accommodate those who need to arrive on Sunday evenings due to distance. We recognise that choosing residential education is a significant decision for families, and we are committed to ensuring it enhances every child’s journey. Through structured routines, nurturing support and a wide range of extra‑curricular opportunities, students build independence, resilience and strong social skills.
Our provision consistently meets and exceeds the national minimum standards for residential special schools, achieving an Outstanding rating in all areas in our most recent Ofsted Social Care inspection, an exceptional endorsement of our commitment to excellence for children and young people with Developmental Language Disorder (DLD).
Students thrive at this residential special school. It is a safe, vibrant and inclusive environment which promotes and enables everyone’s strengths and abilities. The celebration of individual uniqueness and a culture of high aspirations and equal opportunities mean that the students have life-changing experiences.

pageCache.text:
Life in Residential
Residential life at Moor House offers a warm, supportive environment where students can grow in confidence, independence and social skills. When new students arrive, staff provide a thorough induction and each student is paired with an older Buddy-Mentor to help them settle in. Regular contact with home is encouraged, and key workers stay closely connected with families, providing weekly updates.
Every residential student has a dedicated key worker who creates an individual care plan with input from the student and their parents. Through evening activities and one‑to‑one sessions, key workers help develop social communication, independence and therapy targets.
Students enjoy comfortable single rooms that they can personalise with items from home, and waking‑night staff are always available for support. Evenings are active and varied, with a choice of onsite and community-based activities, from swimming and tennis to arts, crafts and horse riding. When not taking part in clubs, students relax with friends in shared common rooms, where they can make snacks, watch TV and continue developing communication skills in a natural, supportive setting. Homework support is available daily, and day students can join some activities too.
Health and wellbeing are well supported: students are registered with the local GP, and the Healthcare team is available across the day and evening. Mealtimes provide additional opportunities for social development, and dietary needs are carefully catered for.
Moor House consistently exceeds National Minimum Standards and is proud to maintain an Outstanding Ofsted Care rating.

Why Moor House?
Residential provision at Moor House School & College enables students to thrive by living, learning and socialising alongside their peers in a nurturing, structured environment. Boarders benefit from high‑quality, individualised care delivered by a skilled team who understand their needs and create a stable home-from-home.
A key strength of our residential provision is the development of confidence and independence. Using our Wheel of Independence™ and Compass of Independence™ programmes, students learn essential life skills, such as personal care, travel, safety, time management, food preparation and budgeting, broken down into manageable, achievable steps. Progress is continually monitored through collaborative working across departments.
Students also build their capacity for positive social interaction and communication. Language-rich opportunities are embedded throughout daily life, from mealtimes and enrichment activities to clubs, games and trips into the community. Off‑site activities such as cinema, theatre, sports, youth groups and outdoor pursuits help broaden experiences and strengthen social confidence.
A strong sense of belonging is central to life at Moor House. Shared routines, traditions, and communal spaces foster connection, wellbeing and pride. Boarders regularly take part in extra-curricular activities, supporting both academic and social development.
Residential life also helps students form lasting friendships and develop positive, supportive relationships with staff. Through guidance, role-modelling and pastoral care, students build emotional resilience and learn strategies to regulate their feelings.
By living away from home in a supportive environment, students gain a head start in personal responsibility, preparing them for future education, employment and independent living.

Moor HouseSchool & College
A specialist school & collegefor children & young people with language disorders.
Moor House School
Moor House School is a charity and non-maintained speech and language specialist school for day and residential students aged 7-19, with placements funded by Local Education Authorities nationwide. We deliver a mainstream curriculum adapted for language needs, with speech and language therapy fully integrated throughout your child’s education. This approach helps students reach their learning potential, build confident communication skills, and grow into happy, independent members of society. Moor House is consistently rated Outstanding by Ofsted.
Moor House College
Moor House College is the co-educational sixth form provision of Moor House School, offering both day and weekly residential placements. Students continue to receive individualised Speech and Language Therapy intervention delivered in 1:1 sessions, small groups and direct classroom support. Occupational Therapy, Physiotherapy, Psychotherapy and Specialist Literacy interventions also continue and are embedded across the curriculum.
Moor House Residential
Moor House Residential offers both day and weekly residential placements for students in year 6 upwards. Our residential provision offers a warm, friendly and inclusive environment where pastoral care and student wellbeing are central to daily life. We aim to create a supportive community in which young people feel safe, valued and able to grow with confidence.
Moor House Research & Training Institute
Moor House Research & Training Institute is a globally recognised centre advancing research, training and resources in speech, language and communication needs, particularly Developmental Language Disorder (DLD). Part of Moor House School & College, it drives evidence-led practice that informs high-quality interventions used in education and clinical settings, led by specialist researchers and clinicians.
Our Story & History
Before it became a school, the original Moor House was owned by the Clutton-Brocks family. During World War 2 it was home to Canadian Air Force Pilots and, later, Italian prisoners of war who worked on local farms.
Dr Cecil Charles Worster-Drought was a neurologist of world renown and Medical Director at the West End Hospital for Nervous Diseases in London. Speech Therapist Mrs Silvia Hudson-Smith was a founder and the first Principal of Moor House until her retirement in 1966.
Moor House opened to students on 21st April 1947 with 21 students aged 5-11 attending by the end of that month. The school was later officially opened by the Right Hon, George Tomlinson, Minister for Education, on 28th June 1947.
An extension comprising classrooms, offices and storage space was added to Moor House in 1951, enabling the number of pupils to rise to 50, also extending the upper age limit to 16.
Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother visited Moor House on 26th November 1953. Her visit was a great success and later, in 1957, she agreed to become the schools Patron. As a consequence, Her Majesty would send a large box of chocolates as a gift to the children each Christmas.
Major building projects
Further extensions including an assembly hall and common rooms, followed by a speech therapy clinic and house for the Principal were completed in 1959 and 1961 respectively, allowing the number of students to rise again to 61.
Swimming pool and fete takings
An outdoor swimming pool was added in 1969 and completed in time for the school fete that year, which raised 782 pounds, 9 shillings and 6 pence.
Main building replaces original Moor House
By 1972, work had also begun on the main quadrangle building we know today. It was a complex, phased build, with three sides complete by 1973 before the old House was demolished and the fourth side added later. The building was officially opened by former Minister of Education Lord Boyle of Handsworth on 24th June 1975.
Parade to celebrate Queen Mother’s 90th birthday
In 1990, Moor House students took part in a parade as part of celebrations for the 90th birthday of our Patron, Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother.
Jubilee celebrations
A Jubilee Fete was held in 1997 to mark the school’s fiftieth anniversary attended my many former pupils, including some of the very first students from 1947. Current and former Principals Mr Flaherty, Mr Lea and Mr Robertson cut the cake!
‘The Countess makes their day’
HRH The Countess of Wessex GCVO succeeded Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother as our Patron and visited the school in successive years in 2003 and 2004 to open a new assessment centre and the new sports and drama centre respectively. In 2011 the School welcomed day students for the first time in its history. Initially, 7 new day students joined 73 boarders. Moor House College opened in 2012, providing sixth form education for the first time alongside a number of partner colleges.
The opening of a college required more residential space, so John Lea House, a residential building for post-16 students named after our former school Principal, was completed in 2012 and officially opened by our Patron The Countess of Wessex.
Our residential campus for junior students, known as ‘The Village’ was completed in May 2016, providing 40 student bedrooms, 3 communal kitchens and dining areas, a Medical & Care Centre and a multi-purpose Student Centre.
Specialist Teaching and Therapy Hub
As we celebrate 75 years Moor House continues to look to the future with the completion of a new, two storey Specialist Therapy Hub.

Forest School
Forest School is part of the curriculum for Moor House School students and takes place in a fully secure site on the grounds of Moor House School & College.
What is Forest School?
Forest School is a student-centred inspirational learning process, that focusses on creating unique learning opportunities through play, exploration, practical skills and creativity. The aim of the Forest School program is to promote the confidence of the individual learners in a natural setting, building self-esteem and resilience through hands-on experiences and championing student’s interests and choices. It is a long-term process that aims to build learner’s confidence and engagement at a comfortable, individual pace.
Where is our Forest School?
Forest School takes place on the grounds of Moor House, within a gated woodland area which branches into surrounding natural areas for further exploration – including the wider site and nearby parks and woodland. Students love to explore and we offer a safe space to allow them to do that.
Why do we need Forest School?
The Forest School ethos encompasses a liberating and captivating route through learning, focussing on promoting risk management, community mindset and practical problems – solving skills that are applicable in every aspect of education. Studies show that acces to the woodland environment and freedom of play, have a hugely positive impact on the attention and listening skills of both young learners and leaders alike!
Exploration and play in the great outdoors promotes physical development, mental and spiritual wellbeing and imaginative learning and helps us all to build stronger connections with local wildlife, our peers and the wider community.
